title: Pauri 30, sound: ekaa maaee

cards: Plenty of languages have a way of starting a story so the listener knows one is coming. Once upon a time. Long, long ago.
In the beginning. A child hears those words and settles in, even before anything has happened. The sound itself says: listen, this is how things came to be.
Pauri 30 of Japji opens with that kind of sound. Four words, two pairs, and the pairs rhyme, so it lands in the ear like the first line of a very old tale.
It's still part of Guru Nanak's answer to the yogis, and it takes a picture they already knew.

teach.b: Here is how Pauri 30 begins: ekaa maaee jugat viaaee, tin chele paravaan. The first pair. Ekaa: one, a single.
Maaee: mother. Ekaa maaee: one mother; hear how the two words lean on the long aa. Then the second pair.

teach.h: JUGAT VIAAEE — BY A JOINING, A BIRTH.
teach.b: Jugat: a way, a method, and also a joining; commentators note it was also a yogi word for technique. Viaaee: gave birth, brought forth. So: by a certain joining, she gave birth.
Now the rhyme: maaee, viaaee. The line swings like a cradle.
Then three more words: tin chele paravaan. Tin: three. Chele: disciples, students, the same word used for a guru's followers.
Paravaan: accepted, approved. One mother, by a joining, brought forth three approved disciples. Who is this one mother?
Commentators answer in different ways. Some read her as maya, the power that makes the visible world. Others hear the Creator's own creative power.
Tomorrow, that, and who the three are. At the end of the stanza, the refrain returns in full: aad aneel anaad anaahat, jug jug eko ves.

teach.h: JUG JUG EKO VES — ONE THROUGH EVERY AGE.
teach.b: The first, the pure, without beginning, unbroken, one form through every age.
It closed pauris 28 and 29 too. Notice how it answers today's opening. The story starts with a birth.
The refrain reminds you who was never born.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 30 is one of four stanzas addressed to the Nath yogis, and like the others it closes with the refrain aades tisai aades and aad aneel anaad anaahat, jug jug eko ves.

o: helpers who cook and serve the shared meal
children, the sons and daughters of a family
disciples, students who follow a guru

games.q: the sound of Pauri 30 — tap the pairs.

s: the two halves of the first line rhyme
maaee and viaaee: it swings like a cradle.
every commentator agrees who the one mother is
some read her as maya; others as the Creator's own creative power.
the refrain says the One was born in the beginning
anaad: without beginning. the story has a birth; the One has none.

games.q: a stanza opens: one mother, by a joining, gave birth. what does she bring forth in Pauri 30?
games.why: tin chele paravaan: three approved disciples. tomorrow, who they are and who sees them.

practice: Say the first line aloud, slowly, three times: ekaa maaee jugat viaaee, tin chele paravaan, letting the rhyme rock, maaee, viaaee, like something you'd say to a child at night.
Then stay quiet: breathe in and silently think ekaa, one; breathe out and think maaee, mother. If your mind drifts, the rhyme will bring you back.

wordCard.voice: Chele, disciples, students. It opens like an ancient tale: one mother, by a joining, gave birth to three approved disciples.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 30: one mother, by a joining, gave birth.

carryVoice: Your line: ekaa maaee. Four words that rock gently, like a cradle. See you tomorrow.
